answer.summary: Ramanujam says founders lose credibility when they present a made-up ROI model after a POC to defend their price. Instead, they should build and validate the model with the customer from day one, making the POC about building a business case.

sections.heading: The mistake
sections.content: Founders often wait until a POC is over, then show up with an ROI model to justify their price. Ramanujam says customers are unlikely to believe a model the founder “just cooked up” and will challenge its assumptions.

sections.heading: What to do instead
sections.content: Co-create the ROI model with the customer from day one: ask about and agree on the inputs—for example, how long a process takes today and how many engineers are involved—and validate those assumptions together. Frame the POC as a way to build a business case, not merely test technical functionality. He says the model can include incremental gains tied to customer KPIs (such as revenue growth or reduced churn), tangible cost savings, and opportunity costs, such as what a team can do with time saved.
